turn_text: Thanks for joining another episode of the Jared Dyson show. This is one of our interview specials this week. We are joined by Congresswoman Virginia Fox. It's a great interview. I'm glad that you've joined us and we're excited to have a special guest here for an interview today. Congresswoman Virginia Fox from North Carolina's fifth congressional district is joining us. Representative Fox, thanks so much for joining us today.
Oh, I'm delighted to be with you, Jared. Thank you for having me.

Yeah, so we'll talk just a little bit. It's an interesting time in our country and a lot of things going on, but you've been in Congress since 2004. And I think that's great that you've represented your area for that long. What caused you to want to run for Congress and stay in Congress?

Well, Jared, very quickly, I grew up in Avery County in the house with no electricity, no running water. Parents my mother had a sixth grade education my father ninth grade education So growing up I had absolutely no aspirations for being public office. I was trying to survive day-to-day You know I was 14 before we had electricity in our house So as you can imagine in those days it was really tough Just surviving so I didn't again didn't grow up with these aspirations But It took me seven years to get my undergraduate degree. And actually, after I went back to school and got my master's degree, I was at a school board meeting one night and the school board was being particularly incompetent. Again, the school board of which I was nonpartisan. I was involved, but not really in politics. Then I had a chance to work for Governor Martin for two years with a friend of mine who was deputy secretary and who was secretary in the Department of Administration. I became deputy secretary. Went there, came back to be president of Maryland Community College. And then I was recruited in 1994 to run for the State Senate by the Republican Party in a district, no Republican had ever won. I did that. I got elected in 1994. And in 2003, Richard Burr announced that he was running for the US Senate from the US House, and people encouraged me to run. So I did. I ran in 2004 and President Bush was running for re-election and I got elected and I've served ever since. I told the President at our rally in March, seems like 100 years ago, we were flying on Air Force One that I'd not lost any of my zeal or enthusiasm for serving and that's absolutely true. I work about 18 hours a day, six and a half days a week, six and a half. But I work very hard six days a week. And then I even work on Sunday nights a lot getting ready for the first of the week. So I just love serving people. And I feel like God gives you opportunities and you must take them I hope this is the highest and best use of my talents, which I readily admit are somewhat limited, but I want to preserve the opportunities I had for other people. There's no reason in the world why I should be in the Congress of the United States with my background. Poor as a church mouse, not no privilege whatsoever. But this is the greatest country in the world when a person like me can get elected to Congress. And so I just want to preserve that opportunity for other people. I got a good education and I worked hard. And that's what this country is all about. We believe that if you work hard, you can achieve success. It doesn't mean you're in elected office.
